points: The $2.6 trillion AI infrastructure spend projected for 2026 gives Intel a large demand pool; if the next print shows data-center AI chip sales gaining traction, the long thesis gets a near-term revenue driver.
Global semiconductor revenue is expected to hit $1.6 trillion in 2026, up 92%, so even modest share gains would translate into materially higher Intel sales over the next year.

If the upcoming report confirms 7nm yields are climbing toward the 90% milestone and cost per wafer is falling toward the sub-$1,000 level, the manufacturing headwind that has crushed margins could ease and the long would have a cleaner 12-18 month path.
After the 2025 margin compression, the next print will show whether operating margins can stabilize above 20%; that is the line between a value trap and a working long.
Management could use the next call to clarify capital allocation and foundry strategy; a credible plan would reduce the execution risk that has kept the stock cheap and support a rerating.
If customer concentration drops toward 30% of revenue, Intel becomes less hostage to one or two big customers, which would make the long position more resilient through 2026.

Asia's 2.9% manufacturing growth in 2026 and ongoing U.S. manufacturing weakness mean Intel must prove it can compete globally; the next few quarters will show whether it is holding share or ceding ground.
AMD and VRT report in late October and early November, and their data-center commentary will either validate Intel's AI opportunity or overshadow it, so positioning now captures that read-through.
